prohibited_recommendations: Do not over-correct sodium (>12 mEq/L per 24 h) — osmotic demyelination risk.
Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy.
required_recommendations: Cautious sodium correction (≤10 mEq/L per 24 h, ideally 6–8 mEq/L) to avoid osmotic demyelination.
Workup SIADH cause — GBS itself is recognised as causing SIADH; identify other contributors (drugs, lung, CNS).
Initiate IVIG / plasma exchange once GBS is supported by EMG and CSF.
MRI brain to exclude central pontine myelinolysis after sodium correction.

avoided_actions.rationale: Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP, presenting with severe SIADH-related hyponatraemia and delayed motor signs

differential.diagnosis: Primary SIADH from CNS / pulmonary / drug cause with secondary encephalopathy
differential.key_features: Profound hyponatremia (Na 110) explains encephalopathy; need to identify primary aetiology (here, GBS-associated SIADH); motor signs emerging on day 6 redirect to a primary neurological cause.
Encephalopathy and seizures possible; CSF cell count and autoimmune encephalitis panel cover; albuminocytologic dissociation favors GBS.
Risk if sodium corrected too quickly; MRI brain shows characteristic pontine lesion; presentation typically delayed 2–6 days.
Liver function unsupportive; ammonia not consistent.
Bilateral symmetric motor signs and areflexia not consistent with focal vascular event; MRI excludes.

key_clinical_evidence: GBS is a recognised cause of SIADH; profound hyponatraemia can dominate the presenting picture and delay diagnosis.
Encephalopathy in hyponatraemia must be distinguished from primary autoimmune encephalitis or osmotic demyelination.
Slow sodium correction protects against central pontine myelinolysis, particularly important once GBS treatment is underway.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: GBS-associated SIADH can produce profound hyponatremia; the appearance of areflexia and ascending weakness after correction unmasks the primary neurological diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute the entire syndrome to hyponatraemia and miss the underlying GBS once motor signs emerge.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. R. is a 64-year-old woman found unresponsive at home by her neighbor. She reported mild malaise, decreased appetite, and mild stomach discomfort the day prior. On emergency evaluation, she was obtunded (GCS 9) with confused speech. Laboratory studies revealed profound hyponatremia with serum sodium 110 mEq/L — markedly below her last documented value of 136 mEq/L three months prior on the same medication regimen. Serum osmolality was 235 mOsm/kg. Urine osmolality 413 mOsm/kg with high urine sodium consistent with SIADH. CT head and neck were normal. MRI brain showed multiple nonspecific T2 hyperintensities without osmotic demyelination. EEG showed mild diffuse slowing — no epileptiform discharges. CSF on day 1 showed protein 52 mg/dL with 1 WBC. Initial management focused on SIADH treatment with hydrochlorothiazide discontinuation, hypertonic saline, and IV antibiotics (empiric). Sodium was corrected from 110 to 120 mEq/L over 24 hours — within safe range (10 mEq/L/24h). By hospital day 5 she was improving cognitively and transferred to the ward. However, on day 6 she complained of new lower back pain followed by bilateral leg numbness and tingling and gait instability. Neurological examination then revealed bilateral lower limb weakness and areflexia — findings not present at admission. The motor and sensory findings emerged on day 6, after correction of the hyponatremia, having been preceded at presentation by the dominant hyponatremic encephalopathy.

neurological_exam.additional: Found unresponsive at home. Serum sodium 110 mEq/L on admission — profound hyponatremia. SIADH confirmed. Hydrochlorothiazide was held on admission but sodium had been stable for 3 months prior on the same regimen. Motor and sensory neurological symptoms emerged on day 6, after sodium correction.
neurological_exam.coordination: Limited by encephalopathy on admission. Day 5+: mild limb ataxia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Intact. No focal cranial nerve deficits on admission. Day 6: bilateral lower extremity weakness identified.
neurological_exam.gait: Gait instability — cannot walk safely without bilateral support (day 6).
neurological_exam.mental_status: Obtunded on admission (GCS 9). Confused. By day 5: improved orientation, conversant.
neurological_exam.motor: Day 6 — bilateral lower limb weakness: hip flexion 3/5, knee extension 3+/5, ankle dorsiflexion 3/5. Upper extremity 4/5. Prior to admission: normal motor strength reported by family.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Day 6 — diminished patellar (1+), absent Achilles bilaterally. Day 1 exam: reflexes were documented as diminished.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral distal tingling and numbness. Reduced light touch in lower extremities.
